interactions.label: Which of the following slit-lamp findings distinguishes granulomatous iridocycli

params.question: Which of the following slit-lamp findings distinguishes granulomatous iridocyclitis from non-granulomatous iridocyclitis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ciliary flush indicates deep ciliary vessel congestion and is common to both granulomatous and non-granulomatous iridocyclitis. It does not differentiate the two types.

answers.text: Fine stellate keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fine stellate KPs are characteristic of non-granulomatous iridocyclitis, typically seen in HLA-B27-associated disease. Their presence actually points away from granulomatous disease.

Mutton-fat KPs and iris nodules — Koeppe nodules at the pupillary margin and Busacca nodules on the iris stroma — are the hallmarks of granulomatous iridocyclitis, seen in sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome.
Posterior synechiae and miosis occur in both forms of iridocyclitis. They reflect inflammation severity, not the granulomatous or non-granulomatous character of the disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the slit-lamp findings: mutton-fat KPs and iris nodules (Koeppe, Busacca) indicate granulomatous disease, while fine stellate KPs without nodules indicate non-granulomatous disease.
Well done. The character of keratic precipitates and the presence of iris nodules are the slit-lamp markers that separate granulomatous from non-granulomatous iridocyclitis.

params.question: A patient on long-term topical prednisolone for chronic iridocyclitis develops raised intraocular pressure with an open anterior chamber angle. Which class of antiglaucoma medication is contraindicated in this patient?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-blockers are safe and effective in uveitic glaucoma. They lower IOP by reducing aqueous production without affecting the inflammatory process.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce aqueous production and are safe in uveitic glaucoma. They do not worsen uveal inflammation.
Alpha-agonists reduce aqueous production and increase uveoscleral outflow without exacerbating uveitis. They can be used safely in uveitic glaucoma.
Prostaglandin analogues worsen blood-aqueous barrier breakdown and increase uveal inflammation. In uveitic glaucoma, they are contraindicated despite being first-line for primary open-angle glaucoma.

overallFeedback.feedback: Prostaglandin analogues are first-line for primary open-angle glaucoma but are contraindicated in uveitis because they worsen blood-aqueous barrier breakdown and exacerbate inflammation.
Correct. Prostaglandin analogues worsen uveal inflammation — always use beta-blockers or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors for uveitic glaucoma.

interactions.label: Which clinical feature best distinguishes hyphema from hypopyon when examining a

params.question: Which clinical feature best distinguishes hyphema from hypopyon when examining a horizontal fluid level in the anterior chamber?

answers.text: Hyphema settles superiorly while hypopyon settles inferiorly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both hyphema and hypopyon settle inferiorly under gravity. The anterior chamber holds only about a quarter of a millilitre, and both form horizontal levels at the bottom.

answers.text: Hyphema appears red (blood) while hypopyon appears white (leucocytes and fibrin)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The colour of the fluid level is the key bedside distinction. Hyphema is red because it contains erythrocytes from vascular injury. Hypopyon is white or creamy because it contains leucocytes and fibrin from inflammatory or infective exudate.

answers.text: Hyphema is always infective while hypopyon is always sterile

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is incorrect in both directions. Hyphema is usually traumatic (not infective), caused by iris root vessel tears. Hypopyon can be sterile (severe iridocyclitis, Behçet disease, TASS) or infective (endophthalmitis).

answers.text: Hyphema is graded by corneal clarity while hypopyon is graded by the proportion of the chamber filled

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hyphema is graded by the proportion of the anterior chamber it fills — from Grade I (less than one-third) to Grade IV (total, the eight-ball hyphema). Corneal clarity is not part of the hyphema grading system.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: hyphema is a red fluid level (erythrocytes from vascular injury) and hypopyon is a white fluid level (leucocytes and fibrin). Both settle inferiorly under gravity.
Correct. Colour is the bedside distinction: red (blood) means hyphema, white (leucocytes and fibrin) means hypopyon. Both settle inferiorly as horizontal levels.

params.question: A patient with recurrent acute non-granulomatous anterior uveitis is found to have inflammatory low back pain and sacroiliitis on imaging. Which systemic condition is most likely associated?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ankylosing spondylitis is an HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthropathy that classically presents with recurrent acute non-granulomatous anterior uveitis and sacroiliitis. It is the most common systemic association of anterior uveitis.
Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous uveitis (mutton-fat KPs, iris nodules), not the non-granulomatous pattern described here. It is associated with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, not sacroiliitis.
Multiple sclerosis is associated with intermediate uveitis (pars planitis), not anterior uveitis. The anatomical site of inflammation links to different systemic conditions.
VKH causes bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with systemic depigmentation. It spans all three uveal zones and does not present as isolated recurrent non-granulomatous anterior disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recurrent non-granulomatous anterior uveitis with sacroiliitis points to HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathy. Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous disease; MS links to intermediate uveitis; VKH causes panuveitis.
Correct. HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, particularly ankylosing spondylitis, are the most common systemic association of recurrent acute non-granulomatous anterior uveitis.

params.question: After diagnosing acute non-granulomatous iridocyclitis in the 28-year-old patient, the ophthalmologist orders HLA-B27 testing despite this being a first episode. Which clinical detail from the history BEST justifies this decision?

answers.text: The presence of ciliary flush rather than conjunctival injection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ciliary flush is a diagnostic sign of iridocyclitis that helps distinguish it from conjunctivitis. It confirms the ocular diagnosis but does not indicate a need for systemic investigation.

answers.text: The unilateral nature of the eye disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anterior uveitis is typically unilateral, even in HLA-B27-associated disease. Unilateral presentation is the expected pattern and does not independently justify ordering systemic investigations.

answers.text: The two-year history of chronic low back pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic low back pain in a young man is a strong clinical clue to spondyloarthropathy, particularly ankylosing spondylitis. This systemic symptom connects the ocular disease to an underlying condition requiring rheumatology referral and disease-modifying treatment.
While anterior uveitis is more common in young adults, age alone does not warrant HLA-B27 testing in a first episode. Many first episodes are idiopathic and resolve without systemic disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: The systemic history is key: chronic low back pain in a young man points to spondyloarthropathy. Ciliary flush confirms the ocular diagnosis but does not drive systemic workup; age and laterality alone do not justify HLA-B27 testing.
Correct. The two-year history of low back pain is the systemic clue that links the eye disease to ankylosing spondylitis and justifies targeted investigation even in a first episode.
